addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

---
name: strix-halo-bench-runs
description: "How the strix-halo-vulkan benchmark suite is run and how long each family takes, plus the run-quality conventions the repo's docs expect."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 6c27486f-644d-4f43-a0b0-6ebe2136679b
  modified: 2026-09-18T12:55:03.680Z
---

`go run ./cmd/bench -blocks 32,64,128,256,512,1024 <family>` — the non-default
block list is what every committed `results/*.csv` was measured with, so keep
it if rows are to stay comparable. `go generate ./...` first if any `.comp`
changed (`*.spv` is gitignored). As of 2026-09-13 the `moe` family is ~9
minutes / 896 rows; it prints its summary tables only at the end, so there is
no progress output to poll — run it in the foreground with a long timeout.
The `bank` family (added 2026-09-15, LLM.md L0a) is the odd one out: its 72
timed cells are seconds, but `go run ./cmd/bench -bankgib 64 -bankreadmib 1024
bank` first allocates 64 GiB in 19 buffers and writes one word per 4 KB page,
which is most of its ~3-minute wall clock. Check `free -g` has the headroom
before starting it.

**A whole-model tok/s number is only comparable against a control run the
same hour** (P1c, 2026-09-18): with an identical binary the decode step
measured 30.51 ms one day and 39.20 the next — every *dense-bank* kernel
1.6-1.9x slower (dn.qkv 115→206 us, head 1964→3531) while every MoE
expert-bank rung was unchanged. Suspected GTT page fragmentation of the
float-staged dense banks (32-day uptime, swap 100% full); unprovable without
root. **And a difference below ~0.5 tok/s needs interleaved A/B/A/B pairs, not one
pair** (P3, 2026-09-18): three pairs of the same two banks gave −0.06, +0.14
and +0.05 tok/s, so either single pair would have reported a signed number
where the truth was a within-arm spread of 0.31 against a real difference of
~0.04. Quote the means and the within-arm spread, not one delta.

So when measuring a decode/prefill change, rebuild yesterday's code in
a worktree (`.spv` are gitignored — regenerate or copy them) and run both
binaries back to back; never quote a delta against a prior day's CSV. Also:
run 1 of a freshly staged graph diverges from runs 2+ at ~1.6e-5 in the
logits (research/p1c-prerecorded-decode.md finding 4) — warm the graph once
before any bitwise comparison.

One-token `-ladder` runs of `cmd/llm` (moe/dn/attn/hc) must defeat the 32 MiB
MALL or every rate is an L3 number: stage many layers and use `-iters 1`
(e.g. `-moe -tokens 1 -ladder -layers 16 -iters 1`, P1b 2026-09-18 —
`ProfileSweep` walks a dispatch kind across layers, so each timing reads a
cold bank). The screen: any CSV row whose gbps exceeds 242 was not measuring
DRAM. The default two-layer, 20-iter form re-reads a ~32 MB working set from
the MALL.

**`go generate` after a `.comp` edit is load-bearing, and skipping it fails
*silently and flatteringly*.** `.spv` is gitignored and embedded into the Go
binary, so an edited shader that was not regenerated runs the **previous**
kernel — and a hand-compile to `/tmp` to check syntax is not the same thing.
On 2026-09-19 (P5b) that produced a whole round of measurements that read as a
2x speed-up and a full set of green tests, because the old kernel was doing
half the work on the new grid. Regenerate just the families touched
(`grep "go:generate" shaders/shaders.go | grep <file>.comp | sed 's|^//go:generate ||'`
into a loop) and check the `.spv` mtime before believing any number.

**Why:** the repo's TODO.md handoffs report a reproducibility figure for every
session (two runs of the family, median ratio and p10-p90 over common rows),
so a session that measures anything is expected to run its family twice and
quote the agreement.

**How to apply:** budget ~20 minutes for two `moe` runs, save each log and CSV
to the scratchpad so run N-1 survives for the comparison, and check nothing
else is using the GPU (`/sys/class/drm/card1/device/gpu_busy_percent`) before
starting. **"Nothing else" includes your own `go build` and `go test`** — a
whole-model decode step is ~3 ms of host work in ~28, and compiling beside a
`-gen` run cost one control pass 1.6 tok/s of 35 (P4c, 2026-09-19), which is
four times the difference such a run is usually measuring. Start the
measurement detached (`setsid nohup … &`, or the foreground loop will kill it
when the tool call times out) and edit *text* while it runs, nothing else. Do not poll with `pgrep -f` — see
[[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]].
---
name: llm-resident-run
description: The whole-model runs (`cmd/llm -resident`, `-graph`, `-gen`, `-ppl`, `cmd/serve -llm`, `TestGraphLogits`) stage 82-83 GB of qwen3.8-flash-next; what they cost in time and RAM, and why nothing else can run beside them.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Since L8a/L8b the dense banks are int8 rather than halves and residency is
81.89 GB with the head** (`-dense` 4.32 GB); `LLM_DENSE_FP16=1` puts every
block back on the old halves and restores the old sizes exactly, which is how
the two are compared. **A decode token is 31.7 ms and residency 79.85 GB as of
L8c-7 (2026-09-17)** with all five 4.5-bit families named in
`LLM_DENSE_BANK` — 40.5 ms at L8e, 33.3 at L8c-6, ~134 before L7d — so `-n 64`
is a ~2.0 s tail on top of staging. Without `LLM_DENSE_BANK` the run is still
L8a's int8 bank at 81.89 GB and 40.5 ms.

**Do not schedule a whole-model run above ~2560 rows**: at 48 layers
`-graph -tokens 3072` (or `-ppl -ctx 4096`) **never returns** — it stalls
inside the driver's submit with one host thread at 100% and the GPU at 2-3%,
and the shim's 20 s fence timeout never fires, so it hangs indefinitely rather
than erroring. 2048 and 2560 are fine; the 4-layer prefix is fine at 4096.
This is a known open question in `LLM.md`, not a mistake to re-discover.

`go run ./cmd/llm -resident` (added 2026-09-16, LLM.md L6a) stages every layer
of all five blocks: **84.20 GB of device buffers (82.40 since L8a), ~35 s wall
clock**, and it
ends with about 41 GB of MemAvailable left on this 117.7 GiB machine. Peak
host memory is separate — the dense blocks dequantise to f32 before packing,
and the 36 DeltaNet layers are 8.35 GB of transient floats at once — which is
why the tool stages dense first and the 77 GB expert bank last.

**Why:** it is the only thing in the repo that takes most of the machine, so a
second GPU or large-allocation job started beside it will either fail to
allocate or perturb the timing it prints. `-bank N,N,...` restages just the
bank, which is the cheap way to vary residency; `-dense` is the 6.8 GB half
and runs in 8 s.

`go run ./cmd/llm -graph` and `go test ./llm/ -run TestGraphLogits` (added
2026-09-16, LLM.md L6b) are the same weight but **85.47 GB**, because they add
the 1.27 GB lm head; `-tokens 2048` adds another ~1.1 GB of arenas. Staging is
~35-40 s, so budget a 1800 s timeout. Both take a `-layers 4` / `GraphOpts{
Layers: 4}` prefix that is 7.4 GB and three seconds — use that while changing
anything about the order, and the full stage only for the gate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -gen` (added 2026-09-16, LLM.md L7c) is the same 85.47 GB
plus the KV cache, and it is the slow one: staging is ~35-50 s and generation
is **~40.5 ms a token** (see above), so `-n 64` is a ~2.6 s tail on top.
**Every committed decode CSV is `-prompt 'The capital of France is'`**; the
flag's default is the 81-token `graphDefaultPrompt`, on which the model emits
EOS at the first step and the decode row is meaningless. A 900 s timeout
covers `-n 64`; a two-minute one does not even cover the staging. `-layers 4`
is 7.4 GB, ~2 s to stage and ~18 ms a token, which is the right thing to use
for anything about the loop rather than about the rate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -ppl` (added 2026-09-17, LLM.md L8c-0) is the longest of
them: 81.89 GB, ~37 s of staging and then **3.3 s per 2048-token chunk for 145
chunks — 7m58s** over `wiki.test.raw`, so run it in the background and wait on
the log rather than holding a foreground timeout. `-chunks N` cuts it (4
chunks is ~15 s after staging) but **only screens for broken**: four chunks
read +0.32% against llama.cpp where the whole corpus reads −0.13%, sign and
all. `-layers 4` plus `-chunks 2` is the 8 GB plumbing check. The reference
side is `llama-perplexity -c 2048 -b 2048`, ~6.5 s a chunk, and it needs the
machine too — never both at once. **`LLM_DENSE_SIM=<plan>` forces the fp16
arm** (L8c-1), so a simulated run is the old 84 GB residency and ~6 s longer
to stage, and its tok/s means nothing — it grades accuracy only.
`LLM_DENSE_SIM_QUANT=imatrix` needs `models/…/imatrix_unsloth.gguf` (the
fetch script gets it; note the source's `_file` suffix) and adds ~10 s of
staging for the nineteen-rung scale search.

**Since P4b/D20 (2026-09-19) a served-default run also stages the MoE bank
narrower, and it is not free at startup.** `LLM_MOE_BANK` (default off in
`cmd/llm`, set to `llm.ShippedMoEBank` by `cmd/serve -llm`) transcodes four
tensor families out of the checkpoint's bytes — 4.2 B weights of
`ffn_down_exps` plus 236 M of the shared expert — so **the MoE block stages
in ~52 s instead of ~25**, and a whole-model run is ~1m32s to first chunk
rather than ~40 s. Residency drops 77.41 -> 76.00 GB in that block (78.53 GB
whole-model with D19's dense bank). Budget the extra minute in every timeout;
`LLM_MOE_BANK=off` is the control.

`go run ./cmd/serve -llm` (added 2026-09-17, LLM.md L9a) is the same residency
held open: **33.5 s to stage at `-llm-ctx 4096`**, ~84 GB, and it then serves
until interrupted. A request is a prefill plus ~44 ms a token (22.7 tok/s
through the server on the L8 banks), so a 48-token answer is under a second.
Start it in the background, poll the log for `listening on`, and **kill it
with `pkill -f '[e]xe/serve'` when finished** — the bracket matters, because
`pkill -f 'exe/serve'` matches the shell running it and kills the session
instead (the same trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]). It holds
the machine for as long as it runs. `-llm-layers 4` is the 7 GB, 3.5 s prefix
and is the right thing for anything about HTTP rather than about the text.

**The access log prints no bodies by default** (`-log-bodies` turns them back
on): a chat server's bodies are conversations. The per-request `llm:` line is
separate and always printed — prompt tokens, how many were reused from the
last turn, and the two rates.

**The model path must name a shard, not the directory.**
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/` now holds three checkpoints — the model, the
imatrix and the MTP head — so `gguf.OpenSet` refuses it as ambiguous and
`cmd/llm`'s own `-model` default no longer resolves. Pass
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf`,
which is what `cmd/serve` defaults to.

**`-layers 24` is the end-to-end instrument when 48 will not fit.** With the
`ai` user service resident (~7 GB) this machine has ~80 GB MemAvailable
against a 48-layer `-graph`'s ~80 GB, which is too tight to schedule. A
24-layer `-graph` is **~40 GB, ~2 min to first number**, and it is a *real*
whole-graph measurement — all five blocks, the head, the host loop, the
per-block ms columns in the CSV — not a block bench. Its one distortion is
that the M-independent fixed costs (head 2.4 ms, `ple`, `move`, host) are 24%
of a step there against 13% at 48 layers, so any *ratio* read off it is
optimistic and the 48-layer number is owed (P5, 2026-09-19).

**How to apply:** run them in the foreground with a long timeout and nothing
else on the GPU, the way [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] asks. `-resident`'s closing
measurement (layer 3's MoE block) is comparable to `-moe -tokens 512 -iters 10`
only at the same iteration count.

expert-bank rung was unchanged. Suspected GTT page fragmentation of the
float-staged dense banks (32-day uptime, swap 100% full); unprovable without
root. **And a difference below ~0.5 tok/s needs interleaved A/B/A/B pairs, not one
pair** (P3, 2026-09-18): three pairs of the same two banks gave −0.06, +0.14
and +0.05 tok/s, so either single pair would have reported a signed number
where the truth was a within-arm spread of 0.31 against a real difference of
~0.04. Quote the means and the within-arm spread, not one delta.

So when measuring a decode/prefill change, rebuild yesterday's code in
a worktree (`.spv` are gitignored — regenerate or copy them) and run both
binaries back to back; never quote a delta against a prior day's CSV. Also:
run 1 of a freshly staged graph diverges from runs 2+ at ~1.6e-5 in the
logits (research/p1c-prerecorded-decode.md finding 4) — warm the graph once
before any bitwise comparison.

One-token `-ladder` runs of `cmd/llm` (moe/dn/attn/hc) must defeat the 32 MiB
MALL or every rate is an L3 number: stage many layers and use `-iters 1`
(e.g. `-moe -tokens 1 -ladder -layers 16 -iters 1`, P1b 2026-09-18 —
`ProfileSweep` walks a dispatch kind across layers, so each timing reads a
cold bank). The screen: any CSV row whose gbps exceeds 242 was not measuring
DRAM. The default two-layer, 20-iter form re-reads a ~32 MB working set from
the MALL.

**`go generate` after a `.comp` edit is load-bearing, and skipping it fails
*silently and flatteringly*.** `.spv` is gitignored and embedded into the Go
binary, so an edited shader that was not regenerated runs the **previous**
kernel — and a hand-compile to `/tmp` to check syntax is not the same thing.
On 2026-09-19 (P5b) that produced a whole round of measurements that read as a
2x speed-up and a full set of green tests, because the old kernel was doing
half the work on the new grid. Regenerate just the families touched
(`grep "go:generate" shaders/shaders.go | grep <file>.comp | sed 's|^//go:generate ||'`
into a loop) and check the `.spv` mtime before believing any number.

**Why:** the repo's TODO.md handoffs report a reproducibility figure for every
session (two runs of the family, median ratio and p10-p90 over common rows),
so a session that measures anything is expected to run its family twice and
quote the agreement.

**How to apply:** budget ~20 minutes for two `moe` runs, save each log and CSV
to the scratchpad so run N-1 survives for the comparison, and check nothing
else is using the GPU (`/sys/class/drm/card1/device/gpu_busy_percent`) before
starting. **"Nothing else" includes your own `go build` and `go test`** — a
whole-model decode step is ~3 ms of host work in ~28, and compiling beside a
`-gen` run cost one control pass 1.6 tok/s of 35 (P4c, 2026-09-19), which is
four times the difference such a run is usually measuring. Start the
measurement detached (`setsid nohup … &`, or the foreground loop will kill it
when the tool call times out) and edit *text* while it runs, nothing else. Do not poll with `pgrep -f` — see
[[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]].

name: llm-resident-run
description: The whole-model runs (`cmd/llm -resident`, `-graph`, `-gen`, `-ppl`, `cmd/serve -llm`, `TestGraphLogits`) stage 82-83 GB of qwen3.8-flash-next; what they cost in time and RAM, and why nothing else can run beside them.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Since L8a/L8b the dense banks are int8 rather than halves and residency is
81.89 GB with the head** (`-dense` 4.32 GB); `LLM_DENSE_FP16=1` puts every
block back on the old halves and restores the old sizes exactly, which is how
the two are compared. **A decode token is 31.7 ms and residency 79.85 GB as of
L8c-7 (2026-09-17)** with all five 4.5-bit families named in
`LLM_DENSE_BANK` — 40.5 ms at L8e, 33.3 at L8c-6, ~134 before L7d — so `-n 64`
is a ~2.0 s tail on top of staging. Without `LLM_DENSE_BANK` the run is still
L8a's int8 bank at 81.89 GB and 40.5 ms.

**Do not schedule a whole-model run above ~2560 rows**: at 48 layers
`-graph -tokens 3072` (or `-ppl -ctx 4096`) **never returns** — it stalls
inside the driver's submit with one host thread at 100% and the GPU at 2-3%,
and the shim's 20 s fence timeout never fires, so it hangs indefinitely rather
than erroring. 2048 and 2560 are fine; the 4-layer prefix is fine at 4096.
This is a known open question in `LLM.md`, not a mistake to re-discover.

`go run ./cmd/llm -resident` (added 2026-09-16, LLM.md L6a) stages every layer
of all five blocks: **84.20 GB of device buffers (82.40 since L8a), ~35 s wall
clock**, and it
ends with about 41 GB of MemAvailable left on this 117.7 GiB machine. Peak
host memory is separate — the dense blocks dequantise to f32 before packing,
and the 36 DeltaNet layers are 8.35 GB of transient floats at once — which is
why the tool stages dense first and the 77 GB expert bank last.

**Why:** it is the only thing in the repo that takes most of the machine, so a
second GPU or large-allocation job started beside it will either fail to
allocate or perturb the timing it prints. `-bank N,N,...` restages just the
bank, which is the cheap way to vary residency; `-dense` is the 6.8 GB half
and runs in 8 s.

`go run ./cmd/llm -graph` and `go test ./llm/ -run TestGraphLogits` (added
2026-09-16, LLM.md L6b) are the same weight but **85.47 GB**, because they add
the 1.27 GB lm head; `-tokens 2048` adds another ~1.1 GB of arenas. Staging is
~35-40 s, so budget a 1800 s timeout. Both take a `-layers 4` / `GraphOpts{
Layers: 4}` prefix that is 7.4 GB and three seconds — use that while changing
anything about the order, and the full stage only for the gate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -gen` (added 2026-09-16, LLM.md L7c) is the same 85.47 GB
plus the KV cache, and it is the slow one: staging is ~35-50 s and generation
is **~40.5 ms a token** (see above), so `-n 64` is a ~2.6 s tail on top.
**Every committed decode CSV is `-prompt 'The capital of France is'`**; the
flag's default is the 81-token `graphDefaultPrompt`, on which the model emits
EOS at the first step and the decode row is meaningless. A 900 s timeout
covers `-n 64`; a two-minute one does not even cover the staging. `-layers 4`
is 7.4 GB, ~2 s to stage and ~18 ms a token, which is the right thing to use
for anything about the loop rather than about the rate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -ppl` (added 2026-09-17, LLM.md L8c-0) is the longest of
them: 81.89 GB, ~37 s of staging and then **3.3 s per 2048-token chunk for 145
chunks — 7m58s** over `wiki.test.raw`, so run it in the background and wait on
the log rather than holding a foreground timeout. `-chunks N` cuts it (4
chunks is ~15 s after staging) but **only screens for broken**: four chunks
read +0.32% against llama.cpp where the whole corpus reads −0.13%, sign and
all. `-layers 4` plus `-chunks 2` is the 8 GB plumbing check. The reference
side is `llama-perplexity -c 2048 -b 2048`, ~6.5 s a chunk, and it needs the
machine too — never both at once. **`LLM_DENSE_SIM=<plan>` forces the fp16
arm** (L8c-1), so a simulated run is the old 84 GB residency and ~6 s longer
to stage, and its tok/s means nothing — it grades accuracy only.
`LLM_DENSE_SIM_QUANT=imatrix` needs `models/…/imatrix_unsloth.gguf` (the
fetch script gets it; note the source's `_file` suffix) and adds ~10 s of
staging for the nineteen-rung scale search.

**Since P4b/D20 (2026-09-19) a served-default run also stages the MoE bank
narrower, and it is not free at startup.** `LLM_MOE_BANK` (default off in
`cmd/llm`, set to `llm.ShippedMoEBank` by `cmd/serve -llm`) transcodes four
tensor families out of the checkpoint's bytes — 4.2 B weights of
`ffn_down_exps` plus 236 M of the shared expert — so **the MoE block stages
in ~52 s instead of ~25**, and a whole-model run is ~1m32s to first chunk
rather than ~40 s. Residency drops 77.41 -> 76.00 GB in that block (78.53 GB
whole-model with D19's dense bank). Budget the extra minute in every timeout;
`LLM_MOE_BANK=off` is the control.

`go run ./cmd/serve -llm` (added 2026-09-17, LLM.md L9a) is the same residency
held open: **33.5 s to stage at `-llm-ctx 4096`**, ~84 GB, and it then serves
until interrupted. A request is a prefill plus ~44 ms a token (22.7 tok/s
through the server on the L8 banks), so a 48-token answer is under a second.
Start it in the background, poll the log for `listening on`, and **kill it
with `pkill -f '[e]xe/serve'` when finished** — the bracket matters, because
`pkill -f 'exe/serve'` matches the shell running it and kills the session
instead (the same trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]). It holds
the machine for as long as it runs. `-llm-layers 4` is the 7 GB, 3.5 s prefix
and is the right thing for anything about HTTP rather than about the text.

**The access log prints no bodies by default** (`-log-bodies` turns them back
on): a chat server's bodies are conversations. The per-request `llm:` line is
separate and always printed — prompt tokens, how many were reused from the
last turn, and the two rates.

**The model path must name a shard, not the directory.**
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/` now holds three checkpoints — the model, the
imatrix and the MTP head — so `gguf.OpenSet` refuses it as ambiguous and
`cmd/llm`'s own `-model` default no longer resolves. Pass
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf`,
which is what `cmd/serve` defaults to.

**`-layers 24` is the end-to-end instrument when 48 will not fit.** With the
`ai` user service resident (~7 GB) this machine has ~80 GB MemAvailable
against a 48-layer `-graph`'s ~80 GB, which is too tight to schedule. A
24-layer `-graph` is **~40 GB, ~2 min to first number**, and it is a *real*
whole-graph measurement — all five blocks, the head, the host loop, the
per-block ms columns in the CSV — not a block bench. Its one distortion is
that the M-independent fixed costs (head 2.4 ms, `ple`, `move`, host) are 24%
of a step there against 13% at 48 layers, so any *ratio* read off it is
optimistic and the 48-layer number is owed (P5, 2026-09-19).

**How to apply:** run them in the foreground with a long timeout and nothing
else on the GPU, the way [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] asks. `-resident`'s closing
measurement (layer 3's MoE block) is comparable to `-moe -tokens 512 -iters 10`
only at the same iteration count.

9. **Pad the strides in the other kernels — answered on the expert bank, open
   everywhere else.** This
   used to be a falsification test that the model predicted would find
   nothing: mechanism 3 looked like it had caught the GEMV kernels red-handed
   (one wave per row, rows a stride apart) until its own ladder measured that
   exact shape at the full bus at every stride. §3.5 changed the prediction —
   the rule is a window, [128, 256] B of gcd, and the real 4-bit weight rows
   sit *below* it — so it became a sweep with an expected win rather than a
   check. §1.8 finding 6 then ran that sweep on the MoE expert bank and it came
   out backwards: at constant traffic the unpadded stride wins at both shapes,
   including down's gcd-64 row, and every pad costs 1.12-2.4x (see item 3's
   note). What is left here is the same sweep on the kernels the `moe` family
   does not cover — the plain GEMV/W8A8/fp16 paths of item 10 — where the
   prediction is now "no effect, and any pad costs its own address span".
10. **IDEAS §1.3/§1.7 — the load-width rule on the other GEMV kernels.**
   fp16 GEMV sits at 75% of its DRAM ceiling and W8A8 at 73%, where W4A8 now
   reaches 101% at every N it was swept at. This is no longer "try wider
   loads and see": §1.7 gives the target width in closed form — make one
   lane-step cover a whole weight row — and it is format-independent, since
   it is about bytes of a row, not weights. A W8A8 row is twice the bytes per
   weight, so its `VEC` is half W4A8's at the same N; an fp16 row is four
   times, so a quarter. §3.4 shrank the expected gain without removing it:
   at the models' real reduction lengths the width that reaches the bus is
   usually the narrowest one, so what is on offer here is these kernels' own
   27% gap, not the 1.43x W4A8 collected at N=8192. §1.8 confirmed that at the
   MoE shapes: across VEC 1-16 the spread is 3-5%.
11. **IDEAS §1.2 — remove the runtime integer divisions** (`pc.N / pc.block`
   and `n / pc.block`) from everything W4A8 did not rewrite: the
   naive/tiled GEMM paths and the old quantized GEMV variants.
   `gemv,naive,q4` is still slower than naive fp32, which is the symptom.
12. **IDEAS §1.6 — the activation-quantize cost W8A8 and W4A8 both hide.**
   Both kernels get `x` quantized on the host, outside the timed loop, and
   W4A8 additionally gets its per-block activation sums for free. A real
   decode step must produce both on-GPU between layers. The sums are one
   extra reduction over N (cheap, and fusable into the quantize pass), but
   it should be measured rather than assumed — it is the one place where
   these numbers are friendlier than production would be.
13. **Still open from §0**: CPU-side submit/fence cost (the half of §4.1 the
   `overhead` family does not measure), and the last ISA question from §6.1
   (is `v_pk_fma_f16` actually emitted, given §0.1's 1.10x packed-fp16
   surprise). `-blocks` is worth re-sweeping only where a block-size effect
   survives warming — in GEMV it does not.
14. **IDEAS §3.7 — rewrite the subgroup reductions**, now that §6.2 has
   measured *why* they lose rather than guessing: bandwidth is linear in
   threads per row (256 → 223.7 GB/s, 64 → 68.5, 32 → 35.7), so the fix is a
   256-thread workgroup doing `uvec4` loads → per-subgroup `subgroupAdd` → a
   small LDS combine, and there is no wave-size knob worth trying first.
   Mechanical, and it deletes a variant the engine should never pick.
15. **Note on a fresh checkout.** `*.spv` is gitignored, so
   **`go generate ./...` is required** before anything runs — the thirteen
   `strided_read` variants and the 30 WMMA ones are each built from a single
   `.comp`. **This session added one**, `shaders/gemm_wmma_q4.comp`, built
   into eight binaries, so a checkout that skips `go generate` will not
   compile `shaders/shaders.go` at all.
   Worth knowing when reading ISA: RADV caches compiled pipelines on disk, so
   `RADV_DEBUG=shaderstats` and `RADV_DEBUG=asm` print **nothing** on a
   second run of the same shader. Set `MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=true`
   alongside them.

Plus **453 MB of host memset a pass** in `DeltaNetGPU.Resize`, the long context's other 0.91 → 0.98. And a ceiling nobody had priced: **speculation stops at 2048 cells**, because `blk.48` states no compress ratio. - **New instrument**: `cmd/llm -depth` (`cmd/llm/bench_depth.go`) — llama-bench's `-d`, adapted to this graph. At each depth it times one **pp** batch of 512 tokens with the cache already that full, then a **tg** run of 64 single-token passes on top of it.

- Context staged at 131,456 cells (~3.6 GB of KV on top of the model); banks set to the shipped dense + MoE plans, i.e. what `cmd/serve -llm` actually serves.

aiTitle: Benchmark LLM performance at various context depths

content.text:
Here's your answer, and it was worth chasing — it's a real misconfiguration on my side, not just "staging is slow."

## What the CPU was doing

It was re-fitting the MoE expert bank from scratch. Specifically `ffn_down_exps` → IQ4_NL: **40 billion weights through a sixteen-scale search**, parallelised across every core. `llm/moebank.go` does this in `parallelFor`, which is why you saw the whole machine pinned.

The sampler I attached caught it exactly:

| t | cores busy |
|---|---|
| 0–30 s | 9 → 26 |
| 50 s onward | **31.0–31.8 of 32, flat** |

5,731 CPU-seconds burned in the first 200 s, of which **9.3 s was sys** — no I/O wait, pure arithmetic. LLM.md D21 prices this fit at "about eight minutes of a 32-core machine," which matches what we were watching.

## Why the API never does it

The transcode is a pure function of (tensor, format, calibration arm), so it's cached on disk. `cmd/serve/main.go:178` points `LLM_BANK_CACHE` at `bank-cache/` beside the checkpoint, and that directory is already populated from earlier server runs — 26 GB, and I checked it's complete: 48/48 files for every family in the shipped plan. The server pays the fit once ever and then reads 22.6 GB off disk, staging in ~1m6s.

The comment at `cmd/serve/main.go:177` says it outright:

> `LLM_BANK_CACHE=` (empty) turns it off; **`cmd/llm` never sets it.**

That's deliberate — `cmd/llm` is the measurement tool, so it re-fits rather than trusting a cache. I launched the benchmark through `cmd/llm` with the *shipped bank plans* but without the cache env var, so every process start paid the full eight-minute fit that the server has paid once and never repeats. Your instinct was right: the CPU load was specific to my benchmark invocation and says nothing about how the model actually serves.

There's a second, smaller offender that no cache covers: the **dense** bank re-fits on every start (`llm/bank_q4.go` has no cache path). I measured it directly — same 16 dense layers, banks off vs on: **8.6 s / 46.9 CPU-s → 17.4 s / 134.6 CPU-s**, a 2.9x CPU increase. Bounded, but it's why even a cached start isn't free.

I've relaunched the sweep with `LLM_BANK_CACHE` set. Staging should drop from ~8 minutes of full-machine CPU to about a minute of disk reads.

aiTitle: Benchmark LLM performance at various context depths

content.text:
Here are the numbers. **Five of the six depths completed; 128000 did not** — I'll explain why below.

## Prompt processing and token generation vs. context depth

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 48 layers, shipped dense + MoE banks (what `cmd/serve -llm` serves), 131,456-cell context, 71.01 GB of weights on the 8060S. `pp` = one 512-token batch with the cache already that full; `tg` = 64 single-token passes on top of it. Corpus is `wiki.test.raw`.

| depth | pp tok/s | vs d0 | tg tok/s | vs d0 | ms/token |
|------:|---------:|------:|---------:|------:|---------:|
| 0 | 541.6 | 1.00x | 24.27 | 1.00x | 41.2 |
| 8,000 | 475.0 | 0.88x | 14.71 | 0.61x | 68.0 |
| 16,000 | 445.9 | 0.82x | 10.68 | 0.44x | 93.6 |
| 32,000 | 378.9 | 0.70x | 6.66 | 0.27x | 150.2 |
| 64,000 | 291.0 | 0.54x | 3.98 | 0.16x | 251.5 |
| 128,000 | — | — | — | — | *run died, see below* |

**The two rates degrade very differently.** Prefill is roughly half-speed at 64k — it's an arithmetic problem, and the extra attention work amortises across 512 rows. Decode falls **6.1x**, because a batch of one pays the whole cache for a single token.

The attribution says exactly where it goes:

| | attention share of GPU time |
|---|---|
| pp @ depth 0 | 25.9% |
| pp @ 64,000 | 56.9% |
| tg @ depth 0 | 36.4% |
| tg @ 64,000 | **86.1%** |

At 64k a decode token spends 13.85 s of its 15.55 s of GPU time (over 64 tokens) in attention alone. MoE is nearly flat in absolute terms — 528 ms → 560 ms per pp batch — so essentially all the loss with depth is attention, despite the QSA sparse selection.

## Why 128,000 is missing

The run died during the fill at ~115k:

```
shim: 43 of 1025 timestamp slots never became ready (first 982, last 1024)
llm: dispatches 0-1023: vk: dispatch sequence failed: VkResult(2)
```

This is **not** a timeout I can raise, and the shim's own comment at `vk/shim.c:690` says so: the fence has already signalled by the time that wait runs, so a slot not ready in ten seconds is never going to be ready. The GPU completed the work and simply never wrote the last 43 timestamps. That's the same driver pathology LLM.md records as P0 for >2560 rows, reached here via depth instead of row count — the shim converts it into an error rather than the 100%-CPU spin it used to be.

The query pool isn't the constraint (2048 slots, the pass asked for 1025). So 128k looks like a real ceiling on this stack today, not a misconfiguration.

Two other caveats worth stating: no CSV was written (it's emitted at the end, and the run never got there — all numbers above are parsed from the log), and this is **one run, not two**. The repo's convention wants a second pass with the agreement quoted, which I haven't done.

## What I'd suggest next

1. **Reach 128k** by making the per-dispatch timestamp marks optional — `DispatchMultiMarked` always requests them, and they're pure instrumentation. Wall-clock tok/s would still be valid; you'd lose the per-block breakdown at that depth only. Small change to `vk/engine.go`, but it touches the engine everything is tuned by, so I didn't do it unilaterally.
2. **Second run** of 0–64k for the reproducibility figure (~10 min).

---
name: llm-bench-needs-bank-cache
description: "Benchmarking cmd/llm on the shipped banks needs LLM_BANK_CACHE set by hand, or every process start re-fits the MoE bank for eight minutes on all 32 cores."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**`cmd/serve` sets `LLM_BANK_CACHE`; `cmd/llm` never does** (the comment at
`cmd/serve/main.go:177` says so outright). So a `cmd/llm` run launched with
`LLM_MOE_BANK` at the shipped plan but no cache path re-fits `ffn_down_exps`
to IQ4_NL from scratch: 40 billion weights through a sixteen-scale search,
`parallelFor` across every core. Measured 2026-09-19: **31 of 32 cores pinned
flat for the whole fit, 5731 CPU-seconds in the first 200 s, sys time 9.3 s**
— all arithmetic, no I/O. LLM.md D21 prices the whole fit at ~8 minutes.

Set it and staging is a disk read instead:

    LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache

With it, a 48-layer stage at 131k cells was **58.5 s total, MoE block 19.4 s**,
71.01 GB of weights + 5.09 GB of arenas. The cache directory is 26 GB and was
already complete for the shipped plan (48/48 files per family). It is keyed on
(tensor, shape, source type, target type, arm, version) and lives inside the
checkpoint's directory — it does **not** hash the source bytes.

**The dense bank has no cache at all** (`llm/bank_q4.go`), so it re-fits every
start no matter what. Measured on the same 16 dense layers: banks off **8.6 s
wall / 46.9 CPU-s**, dense bank on **17.4 s / 134.6 CPU-s** — 2.9x the CPU.
That part is unavoidable today.

**Why:** the CPU storm looks alarming and looks like inference gone wrong — it
is neither. It is startup-only weight preparation, which is why the served API
never shows it: the server pays the fit once ever and then holds the model
resident. During real inference the GPU sits at 98-99% and host cost is ~3 ms
of a ~31 ms token.

**How to apply:** set `LLM_BANK_CACHE` in every `cmd/llm` invocation that also
sets `LLM_MOE_BANK`, and budget ~60 s of staging rather than ~8 minutes. See
[[llm-resident-run]] and [[strix-halo-bench-runs]].
EOF

    shim: 43 of 1025 timestamp slots never became ready (first 982, last 1024)
    llm: dispatches 0-1023: vk: dispatch sequence failed: VkResult(2)

which is the P0 pathology LLM.md records for >2560 rows, reached by *depth*
instead of row count. **Raising the deadline is not the fix** — `vk/shim.c:690`
argues the fence has already signalled, so a slot not ready in ten seconds
never will be. The query pool is not the constraint either (2048 slots, the
pass asked for 1025). The untried route is making the per-dispatch marks
optional: `DispatchMultiMarked` always requests them and they are pure
instrumentation, so wall-clock tok/s would survive losing the per-block
breakdown at that depth.

and do not schedule a depth sweep past ~115k cells without dealing with the
marks first. Needs `LLM_BANK_CACHE` — see [[llm-bench-needs-bank-cache]].

Prefill halves by 64k; decode falls 6.1x, and the attribution puts essentially all of it in attention (36.4% → 86.1% of GPU time for decode) while MoE stays flat.

**Your CPU question, answered:** `cmd/serve` sets `LLM_BANK_CACHE`, `cmd/llm` never does. My first launches re-fitted `ffn_down_exps` to IQ4_NL from scratch — 31 of 32 cores pinned, 5731 CPU-seconds in 200 s, 9.3 s of it sys. Setting the cache dropped staging from ~8 minutes to 58.5 s. The API never shows this because the server pays the fit once ever; during real inference the GPU runs at 98–99%.

**Left on disk:** `depth-results.csv`, `depth-run1.log`, and the `cpu.samples` trace in the scratchpad. `cmd/llm/bench_depth.go` plus the flag block in `cmd/llm/main.go` are uncommitted in your tree — your auto-committer will take them on the next tick unless you'd rather they didn't. Two memories saved.

**Not done, and they're your call:**
- **128k.** It's a genuine ceiling, not my misconfiguration — the shim's own comment rules out raising the deadline, and the query pool isn't the limit. The untried route is making `DispatchMultiMarked`'s timestamps optional, which would preserve wall-clock rates and lose only the per-block breakdown at that depth. It touches the engine everything is tuned by, so I didn't do it unprompted.
- **A second run.** These are one-run figures; the repo's convention wants a pair with the agreement quoted. About 10 minutes for 0–64k now that staging is a minute.
